opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I went back and forth on quite a bit, because for most of my career the implicit model of impact was pretty institutional. You're inside an organization, you're producing research that feeds into grantmaking decisions or strategy, and the "customer" for your thinking is a fairly small set of people who are going to act on it directly. That's a very legible theory of impact, and I think it's a good one in a lot of cases.

But over time I started to feel that some of the most important bottlenecks weren't about a small group of decision-makers having the right internal analysis. They were more about the broader conversation: how a lot of people, including policymakers, journalists, technical researchers, and just thoughtful members of the public, are forming their picture of where AI is going and how fast. A lot of that picture gets shaped by whoever is writing clearly and regularly in public. If people who've thought hard about forecasting and risk aren't part of that conversation, it doesn't wait for them. It just proceeds without them.

So part of it was a bet that public writing has a kind of compounding, diffuse impact that's harder to measure but potentially larger. You write something, it gets picked up, someone builds on it, it shows up in a policy memo you'll never see. You give up some of the tight feedback loop of "I wrote this and this specific decision changed," in exchange for more surface area.

The other part was honestly about the kind of thinking I wanted to be doing. Writing for a public audience forces me to say what I actually believe, with my uncertainty attached, rather than hedging everything into institutional language. I think that's valuable in itself. A lot of the AI discourse is polarized between "this is all hype" and "we're definitely doomed," and there's real value in someone saying, "Here's my probability distribution, here's why, and here's what would change my mind." Doing that in public, repeatedly, lets people track how my views move as the evidence comes in, and I think that kind of transparency is useful.

I'll be honest that there's real uncertainty in the bet. It's quite possible the counterfactual impact of one more Substack is smaller than I hope, and I try to check in on that periodically. But at the moment, it feels like a moment where clear public thinking about AI timelines and risks is unusually high leverage, and that tipped it for me.

r001.rationale: Cotra describes her choice as partly driven by the kind of thinking she wanted to do and says that public writing is valuable in itself, conveying a reason beyond impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so impact was really the central consideration, and honestly it was the thing I went back and forth on the most. I'd spent a long time at Open Philanthropy, and the case for staying was pretty straightforward: you're sitting next to a lot of money, you have institutional credibility, and when you write something internally it can translate fairly directly into grants and into how the organization thinks about the whole field. That's a very legible form of impact, and it's hard to walk away from.

But over time I started to feel that the thing I was actually best at, and the thing that was most scarce, wasn't the grantmaking per se. It was the writing and the reasoning, trying to lay out, in a lot of detail, how I think about timelines, how I think about what the transition to transformative AI might look like, where the key uncertainties are. And I noticed that the pieces of my work that seemed to have the most outsized effect were the public-facing ones, the things that people outside Open Phil could actually read, argue with, build on, and be influenced by. Inside an institution there's a lot of friction around that. Not in a bad way, it's appropriate for an organization to be careful about what it says publicly, but it meant that a huge fraction of my thinking just never left the building.

So the bet I'm making with the Substack is roughly: the marginal value of one more person doing careful, honest, fairly technical public reasoning about where AI is going is quite high right now, higher than I would have guessed a few years ago. The conversation has gotten a lot bigger, a lot of people are forming views very quickly, and I think there's a real gap between the very polished, somewhat sanitized institutional outputs on one hand and very hot takes on the other. There's room for something in between, where you show your work, you say what you're confused about, and you update in public.

The other piece is that independence changes what I'm able to say. I can be more speculative, I can disagree with people I respect without it being read as the organization's position, and I can follow questions wherever they go rather than where they're most actionable for a funder. I think a lot of the most important questions right now are not immediately actionable, they're more like, what world are we actually heading into, and I wanted the freedom to sit with those.

Of course there's a real cost. I have less leverage over resources, and I'm aware that writing can feel impactful without actually being impactful, you get a lot of feedback and attention and it's easy to confuse that with changing anything. So I try to keep asking myself whether the thing I'm writing would actually shift what a thoughtful person at a lab, or in government, or deciding what to work on, would do. If the answer is consistently no, that's a signal I should rethink. But so far my sense is that it's been the right call, or at least a reasonable experiment.

r001.rationale: She describes choosing independence partly for the freedom to pursue speculative, non-actionable questions and say what she thinks, alongside impact considerations.

astra-6.text:
Impact was a big part of how I thought about it, but I didn’t have a very precise story where I could say, “This particular essay will cause this particular good outcome.” It was more that I had a bunch of things I wanted to think through, especially about AI, and writing publicly seemed like a way to clarify my own thinking while potentially helping other people think through those questions too.

And there was also a personal component: I wanted more space to follow my curiosity and figure out what I actually thought. I don’t think those considerations are necessarily separate from impact. Whether you’re excited about the work, and whether it gives you room to develop ideas you wouldn’t otherwise develop, matters for how useful the work ends up being. So I thought of it as an experiment, with some uncertainty about where the value would come from.

r001.rationale: She describes wanting space to follow her curiosity and develop her own ideas alongside impact, conveying that career choices could include considerations beyond impact alone.

sol-6.1.text:
Impact was a big part of how I thought about it, but I didn’t have a very crisp calculation where I could say, “Writing on Substack is the highest-impact thing I could do.” It was more that I thought there were important questions around AI where I might have something useful to contribute, and writing independently would give me room to explore those questions and see what resonated.

I also wanted to take seriously what I was excited to do. That’s relevant to impact, because it affects whether you’ll keep working on something and whether you’ll do it well. So I saw it as an experiment: give myself some space to write, learn what I’m good at in that format, and then reassess based on whether it seems useful.

r001.rationale: She describes impact as one consideration while also taking her own excitement into account when choosing to write independently, conveying room for career decisions beyond impact alone.
